summary: This standards-track memo specifies RTP payload formats for carrying ETSI Distributed Speech Recognition features (the ES 202 050, 202 211 and 202 212 front-ends). They let speech features be sent over the Internet so recognition can be done remotely.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of sending your whole voice, a phone sends a compact summary of sounds to a computer that figures out the words. This document says how to put that summary in internet packets.

questions: rtp payload for distributed speech recognition
how big is an etsi dsr frame pair
what are the dsr es202050 media subtypes
how does rtp carry speech recognition features
subtitle: How to carry ETSI speech-recognition feature data in RTP packets, so a thin device can leave the recognizing to a server.

tldr.problem: In distributed speech recognition, a small device extracts features from speech and a remote server recognizes the words. Three newer ETSI front-ends (ES 202 050, ES 202 211 and ES 202 212) had no standard way to travel in RTP packets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the RTP layout of RFC 3557 and defines the bit layout of a frame pair (two 10 ms frames, 20 ms of speech) for each front-end: 12 octets for ES 202 050 and 14 octets for the two extended ones. It also registers the media subtypes dsr-es202050, dsr-es202211 and dsr-es202212.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It adds no new security services beyond those of RTP and its profiles.

today: RFC 4060 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2005. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the earlier packetization in RFC 3557.

sections.title: Distributed Speech Recognition over RTP
sections.content:
In distributed speech recognition (DSR), a remote device acts as a thin client (the front-end) and talks over the network to a speech recognition server (the speech engine). The client does not send audio. It sends features computed from the speech.

ETSI first published a DSR front-end standard, ES 201 108, in early 2000, and RFC 3557 defines its RTP packetization. ES 202 050 is a later Advanced front-end that gives substantially better recognition when there is background noise. Its frame format differs slightly from ES 201 108, so the two do not inter-operate.

ES 202 211 and ES 202 212 extend the two earlier front-ends. They add pitch and voicing information so the speech can be reconstructed for human listening, and so recognition of tonal languages can improve. This RFC defines RTP payload formats for all three: ES 202 050, ES 202 211 and ES 202 212.

The RFC also warns that recognizers are extremely sensitive to consecutive frame losses. On a session with high packet loss it suggests limiting the number of frames per packet, or using FEC or interleaving.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone can describe the sounds it hears in a short code instead of sending the whole recording. This document is the rule book for putting those codes into packets so the listening computer can read them.

sections.title: The Three ETSI Front-ends
sections.content:
The ES 202 050 Advanced front-end produces an output vector every 10 ms. It reduces noise with two stages of Wiener filtering, calculates mel-cepstral features, and applies blind equalization. The output is 12 cepstral coefficients plus C0 and log Energy. It also does voice activity detection (VAD), so each frame is marked speech or non-speech and the server may optionally drop non-speech frames. It supports three raw sampling rates: 8 kHz, 11 kHz and 16 kHz.

The features are quantized with split-vector quantization to reduce the data rate. The quantized vectors of two consecutive frames are then placed together in one frame pair (FP).

The ES 202 211 Extended front-end extends ES 201 108. Its feature extraction is the same, but it adds fundamental frequency (perceived as pitch) and a voicing class such as non-speech, voiced, unvoiced or mixed. The pitch of the first frame in a pair is quantized to 7 bits and the second is differentially quantized to 7 bits. The voicing class takes one bit per frame. The extension for a pair is 14 bits plus 2 bits of CRC.

The ES 202 212 Extended Advanced front-end is the same kind of extension, applied to the Advanced front-end of ES 202 050.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways for a device to summarize speech. One cleans up noisy sound first, and two add the pitch of the voice so a computer could even play the speech back.

sections.title: Common RTP Rules
sections.content:
The three formats share their behavior. Any number of frame pairs MAY be put in one RTP payload, and they MUST be consecutive in time. The payload SHOULD stay smaller than the MTU to avoid IP fragmentation, and the sizing advice in Section 3.1 of RFC 3557 applies. The discontinuous transmission rules of Section 3.2 of that RFC apply too.

The RTP timestamp is the sampling instant of the first sample of the first FP in the packet. Its clock rate equals the sampling rate, so it counts samples. One FP lasts 20 ms, which is 160, 220 or 320 samples at 8, 11 or 16 kHz, so the timestamp rises by 160, 220 or 320 per consecutive FP.

The payload is always a whole number of octets. The RTP padding bit (P) may be used if padding is needed for another purpose. The marker bit (M) MUST be set following the general audio codec rules of RFC 3551. The RFC assigns no payload type: the RTP profile in use is expected to assign one or bind it dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet holds a stack of 20 millisecond slices of speech in time order. The timestamp tells the receiver how far along the slices are.

sections.title: Frame Pair Formats
sections.content:
A packet is a standard RTP header followed by a series of frame pairs, using the layout of Section 3 of RFC 3557. What changes is the layout of each pair.

For ES 202 050, two quantized 10 ms mel-cepstral frames are grouped and protected by a 4-bit CRC, forming a 92-bit FP. It MUST be padded with 4 zeros to reach an octet boundary, so each FP is 96 bits, or 12 octets. The frame data includes the codebook indices and a VAD flag for each frame.

For ES 202 211 and ES 202 212, the FP is 112 bits, or 14 octets. It holds the two frames of codebook indices (88 bits), a 4-bit CRC over those 88 bits, the pitch indices Pidx1 (7 bits) and Pidx2 (5 bits), one class bit per frame (Cidx1 and Cidx2) and a 2-bit PC-CRC over the 14 pitch and class bits. That is 44 + 44 + 4 + 7 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 108 bits, plus 4 bits of zero padding. The CRCs MUST be calculated with the formulas in the relevant ETSI standard.

A Null FP marks the end of a transmission segment. For ES 202 211 and ES 202 212 all 112 bits are zero. For ES 202 050 the first 88 bits are zero, followed by the normally calculated 4-bit CRC and 4 padding zeros. This padding is separate from RTP P-bit padding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each slice is a small box with a fixed set of labelled compartments, a check number to catch mistakes, and a few empty bits at the end so the box ends on a neat edge.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP
sections.content:
Three audio subtypes are registered: dsr-es202050, dsr-es202211 and dsr-es202212. There are no required parameters. The optional rate gives the speech sample rate with valid values 8000, 11000 and 16000 (8000 if absent). The optional maxptime defaults to 80 ms, and ptime is also allowed. A session that expects high packet loss MAY choose a shorter maxptime.

In SDP, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name and rate as the clock rate. The ptime and maxptime values go in the matching attributes. All parameters are declarative, so the normal offer/answer usage of RFC 3264 is followed. Congestion control for RTP MUST be used per RFC 3550 and any applicable profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of summary gets its own name tag, so the two ends of a call can agree which one they are using.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Implementations are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and of any RTP profile in use, such as RFC 3551. The payload formats do not specify any different security services.
sections.plainLanguage: These packets are protected the same way as any other call packets, and this document adds no extra locks.

fields.name: Frame 1 indices
fields.desc: Codebook indices of the first 10 ms frame.

fields.name: Frame 2 indices
fields.desc: Codebook indices of the second frame.

fields.name: PC-CRC
fields.desc: Calculated over the 14 pitch and class bits.

fields.name: Padding
fields.desc: Zeros to reach an octet boundary.
